Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the MediCore Health Systems Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers' presentation, there will be a question-and-answer session. As a reminder, please do not place your line on hold as this creates noise in the conference. Today's conference is being recorded. If you have any objections, please disconnect at this time. Finally, as operator instructions indicate, if asked to do so, please press * then 1 on your touchtone phone to ask a question.

I would now like to turn the call over to Sarah Thompson, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you, operator. Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining us today to discuss MediCore Health Systems' financial results for the third quarter of 2024. Joining me on the call are Alex Rivera, Chief Executive Officer; Tom Hargrove, Chief Financial Officer; and Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that certain statements made during this call may contain forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements are based on management's current expectations and are subject to risks, uncertainties, and other factors that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. I'm pleased to report on our performance for the third quarter. We continue to execute on our strategic priorities, focusing on delivering high-quality patient care, expanding our network, and improving operational efficiency.

Today, I will provide an overview of our key achievements during the quarter, focusing on four key aspects: same-facility admissions and patient day growth year-over-year and quarter-over-quarter, labor costs as a percentage of revenue, status of ongoing or planned acquisitions and divestitures, and trends in inpatient versus outpatient volumes.

Let's start with same-facility admissions and patient day growth. These metrics exclude contributions from recent tuck-in acquisitions, like the five-hospital cluster in the Midwest we closed earlier this year, giving us a clear view of organic performance across our 180-hospital footprint. On a same-facility basis, admissions increased 2.8% year-over-year and 1.4% quarter-over-quarter. Patient days, which reflect acuity and length-of-stay trends, grew more strongly at 3.4% YoY and 2.1% QoQ. This continues our streak of six straight quarters of positive growth in both areas, signaling strong post-pandemic recovery and the success of our initiatives.

Elective procedures have been a standout, with orthopedic admissions—such as total joint replacements and spine surgeries—up 5.2% YoY, thanks to pent-up demand and partnerships with ambulatory surgery centers affiliated with groups like United Surgical Partners International. Our case mix index rose to 1.82 from 1.76 a year ago, as we emphasize higher-acuity work like complex cardiovascular and neurosurgeries. This drove patient days higher, with average length of stay up 0.5 days to 4.7 days.

Seasonal factors boosted QoQ results, including a 12% rise in respiratory admissions from Q2, consistent with early flu season patterns reported by peers like HCA Healthcare. Emergency department observation admissions grew 4.1% YoY, aided by AI-driven triage in our Epic MyChart system, which cut door-to-doctor times by 18% and improved conversions to inpatient care.

Regionally, our Southeast operations—42% of beds—led with 4.2% YoY admissions growth, supported by Medicaid redetermination benefits in Florida and Texas, where value-based contracts with Humana and Centene are paying off. Patient days there expanded 5.1% YoY, boosted by oncology expansions like proton therapy centers in Atlanta and Dallas. In the Northeast, representing 25% of capacity, growth slowed to 1.1% YoY due to nursing shortages, but we've countered with 22% reductions in travel nurses from peaks and retention bonuses that lowered annualized nurse turnover to 14% from 19%.

Our hospital command centers, now in 65% of facilities, have optimized bed turnover by 11% using predictive analytics from Cerner Millennium upgrades and Qventus partnerships. The MediCore Virtual Care platform increased admissions from telehealth handoffs by 7% YoY, especially in rural areas. We're shifting to high-margin, high-acuity care, targeting 15% of inpatient volume in bundled payments by year-end, similar to Tenet Healthcare's approach. Revenue per admission climbed 4.6% YoY to $14,200. For Q4, we anticipate 2.5-3.5% YoY admissions growth and 3.0-4.0% for patient days, barring unusual flu activity or CMS IPPS changes. With $450 million in capex for service lines, we're set to outperform peers like Community Health Systems amid Medicare Advantage pressures.

Next, labor costs as a percentage of revenue, our biggest expense at around 55-60% industry-wide. In Q3, this stood at 56.2%, up 210 basis points YoY from 54.1% and 80 basis points sequentially from Q2. This follows peaks like 58.7% during Omicron, but pressures are easing. Absolute labor expenses rose 7.2% YoY to $1.42 billion, with salaried clinical wages up 5.8%—nurses at $48.50 per hour from $45.90—and premium pay for agency staff up 12.4%, though they now cover just 8.2% of nursing hours versus 14.5% in 2022. Revenue growth of 6.1% offered some offset, but higher-acuity inpatient shifts demanded tighter RN ratios, like 1:4 in California under AB 394.

Compared to benchmarks, we're around the 56-58% sector average from Kaufman Hall reports, near HCA's 54.8% and Tenet's 57.1%. Wage inflation has slowed to 4-6% from 15-20% peaks, with travel rates down 23% YoY to $92 per hour per Aya data. Our nursing vacancy is 4.2%, better than the 7.1% national average but above pre-pandemic 2.8%. Physician labor, 22% of total, grew 3.9% YoY via IMG hires and mid-levels like NPs and PAs, handling 28% of primary care.

Geographically, Sunbelt areas like Florida and Texas—42% of beds—saw 57.8%, hit by competition and costs, intensified by CON reforms. Midwest and Northeast—35% of beds—held at 54.9%, aided by low unionization (12% vs. 22% national) and incentives like Ohio's loan forgiveness. California, 15% of footprint, was at 61.3% due to staffing laws and retrofits, but retention bonuses reclaimed 150 basis points.

Mitigation efforts include AI scheduling via LeanTaaS iQueue in Epic MyChart, cutting overtime 18% QoQ and saving $14 million across 72% of hospitals, aiming for 85% by year-end. Telehealth at 22% of outpatient encounters reduced on-site RN hours 11% in ASCs. Our internal Apex Academy—wait, our MediCore Academy—graduated 1,200 LPN-to-RN staff, dropping agency use 420 bps YoY. AMN partnerships secured 15% locums discounts, and retention perks like $5,000 bonuses lifted 12-month rates to 89% from 82%.

We see this peaking at 56.5% in Q4 before 55.8% for the year, with 2-3% wage growth and CMS's 2.9% IPPS update. Robotics investments like da Vinci Xi could trim 50-75 bps long-term. Risks are union pushes or H-1B limits, but vertical integration with SNFs targets sub-54% by 2026, driving 300-400 bps EBITDA gains.

Turning to the status of ongoing or planned acquisitions and divestitures, M&A is central to accelerating high-margin growth, vertical integration, and portfolio optimization amid labor pressures and 35% Medicare Advantage penetration nationally. Kaufman Hall notes hospital margins squeezed 8-10% YoY.

Ongoing deals include the $450 million Coastal Surgical Partners acquisition—12 ASCs and three imaging centers in Florida and Texas—on track for year-end close post-CMS and CON approvals. It adds $220 million revenue at 28% EBITDA margins, with $35 million synergies from shared services, Epic revenue cycle, and payer leverage. Florida's ASC boom, up 15% YoY on site-neutral payments, taps a $10 billion market.

The $320 million Midwest Behavioral Health buy—seven psych facilities and 20 clinics in Ohio and Indiana—eyes Q1 2025 close after antitrust review, adding $180 million revenue at 18% margins amid 22% demand surge per SAMHSA. RevOptix AI has cut bad debt 12% in pilots.

Tuck-ins closed: two Atlanta ortho groups with 45 providers adding $45 million revenue at $1.2 million per physician, and a rural Georgia home health agency for 2,500 patients, beating plans under 40% value-based contracts.

Divestitures: Sold two low-occupancy rural Kansas/Nebraska hospitals (under 35%, negative margins post-5% Medicaid cuts) for $120 million cash, $40 million gain, redeployed to ASCs. Advanced talks for five Pacific Northwest SNFs ($90 million revenue) at 10x EBITDA by Q2 2025, shifting to 15%+ margin home health/hospice as PDPM compresses SNFs to 4-6%.

Planned M&A leverages $2.5 billion capital across 15 LOIs: 20-25 ASCs in 18 months for musculoskeletal/GI in Phoenix/Dallas (under 30% penetration); physician/ancillaries for 60% employed mix by 2026 vs. 48%, countering 7% provider shortage; digital health like R1 RCM for $15 billion AR automation.

Southeast focus (45% beds) with 1.5%+ growth and strong commercial payers; de-emphasize Midwest for Sun Belt/Texas like Tenet. Scale yields 200-300 bps payer edges ($2,450 net revenue per ADC vs. peers' $2,300). HorizonOne telehealth/RPM rollout boosts acquired utilization 10-15%. M&A to add 12-15% FY24 revenue growth, 12%+ ROIC. Subject to regulatory risks.

Finally, trends in inpatient versus outpatient volumes. This shift accelerates with CMS site-neutral policies, 51% Medicare Advantage penetration, and preferences for convenience. Inpatient admissions hit 142,000, down 3.2% YoY or 4,700 fewer; adjusted patient days fell 2.8% to 1.1 million—fifth straight quarter of moderation, like HCA's 2-3% Q1 dip. Outpatient encounters rose 6.8% YoY to 2.45 million, procedures up 9.2%, revenue per visit +1.5% to $1,420 on acuity migration.

Ortho: inpatient down 8.1%, ASC joints up 15.4% to 62% of volume (from 48%), da Vinci in 18 ASCs cuts ALOS to <4 hours, complications <1.2%. Cardiology: outpatient caths +7.6%, inpatient -4.5% via Medtronic CareLink. Oncology infusions +5.9% in 35 centers under UnitedHealthcare bundles.

Sunbelt (58% beds, Texas/Florida): inpatient -1.9%, outpatient +8.4% on MA density >55%, CON reforms, Medicaid unwind. Northeast (22%, PA/NY): inpatient -5.7%, outpatient +4.2% despite No Surprises Act. Rural (15%): inpatient +1.2% via CAH/tele-stroke diverting 22%.

We're investing $450 million Capex (35%) in three new ASCs (Houston/Phoenix/Orlando) for 20,000 procedures at 25-30% margins like Tenet's Conifer. Optum JV in 12 markets grows risk-adjusted outpatients 12% YoY at 18% MA capture. Oracle Cerner AI diverts 85% low-acuity cases, +14% throughput.

FY24 outlook: inpatient -2-4%, outpatient 7-9%, +2-3% EBITDA per visit on OPPS 2025. 42% commercial/28% MA buffers 9.2% RN vacancies (down from 14%) and sequestration risks. Outpatient now 41% revenue vs. 32% in 2021, positioning us like Community Health Systems' pivot—accretive growth.

Now, I’ll turn the call over to Tom Hargrove to provide a more detailed review of our financial results.

Tom Hargrove:
Thank you, Alex. Good morning, everyone. As Alex highlighted, we had a solid quarter. Net revenue for Q3 2024 was $2.75 billion, an increase of 7.2% compared to the same period last year. This growth stemmed from higher patient volumes, favorable payer mix, and the trends Alex outlined.

Our operating expenses were $2.35 billion, representing 85.5% of net revenue. We're maintaining tight cost controls while investing in growth areas like outpatient expansion and tech upgrades.

Net income for the quarter was $195 million, or $1.38 per diluted share. Adjusted EBITDA reached $425 million, up 9% YoY. We're pleased with this performance and confident in hitting our full-year guidance, with leverage from M&A and volume shifts supporting margin expansion.

Now, I'd like to turn the call back to Alex Rivera.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, Tom. At this time, we will open the call for questions.

Operator:
Thank you. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

John Smith:
Good morning, team. Can you provide more color on the impact of Medicare Advantage reimbursement changes on your operations?

Alex Rivera:
Good morning, John. Absolutely. Medicare Advantage now represents a significant portion of our payer mix, around 28-30% system-wide, and recent reimbursement scrutiny has been a focus. We've seen some moderation in MA volumes in select markets due to plan restructurings, but our value-based contracts with major payers like Humana and UnitedHealthcare have insulated us, covering over 40% of at-risk lives. In the Southeast, where MA density exceeds 55%, we've captured tailwinds from redeterminations, contributing to our 4.2% admissions growth there. Strategically, our bundled payment models—targeting 15% of volume—align incentives, and AI tools like RevOptix have reduced denials by 12%. We expect any CMS adjustments to be manageable, with our 42% commercial mix providing a strong buffer. Lisa, any operational add?

Lisa Chen:
Yes, John. Operationally, our command centers and predictive analytics have optimized throughput amid these shifts, turning potential headwinds into opportunities for higher-acuity care.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Maria Lopez with J.P. Morgan. Please go ahead.

Maria Lopez:
Thanks. What are your expectations for patient volume growth in the next quarter, considering the current environment?

Tom Hargrove:
Hi, Maria. For Q4, we're guiding same-facility admissions to 2.5-3.5% YoY and patient days 3.0-4.0%, assuming normalized seasonality and no major disruptions. Outpatient should accelerate to 7-9%, driven by ASC ramps and procedure demand, while inpatient moderates 2-4%. Labor deleveraging and M&A closes will support this, with revenue growth of 7-9% overall.

Operator:
Our next question is from David Kim with Barclays. Please go ahead.

David Kim:
Good morning. On the M&A front, how are you thinking about integration risks with the Coastal deal, especially around payer contracts?

Alex Rivera:
Morning, David. Integration is key, and we've got proven playbook from prior tuck-ins. For Coastal, shared services and Epic RCM will deliver those $35 million synergies quickly. Payer leveraging from our scale—200-300 bps better rates—positions us well in Florida's site-neutral environment. We've started pre-close tech pilots, and ROIC targets remain above 12%. Tom?

Tom Hargrove:
Spot on. Funding via revolver and cash keeps balance sheet strong, with pipeline robust at $2.5 billion deployable.

Operator:
Thank you. This concludes the question-and-answer session. I'll now turn the call back to Alex Rivera for closing remarks.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you for the questions. In closing, I want to thank our dedicated employees for their hard work and commitment to providing high-quality care to our patients. We remain focused on executing our strategic priorities and delivering long-term value to our shareholders.

Sarah Thompson:
Thank you for your participation in today's call. This concludes the MediCore Health Systems Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. You may now disconnect.
